claims.text: Local compositional heterogeneity at the surface governs the premelting behavior of high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Surface compositional heterogeneity creates regions with reduced cohesive energy.
Regions with reduced cohesive energy initiate melting at lower temperatures.
Thermal annealing reduces surface compositional heterogeneity.
Reducing surface compositional heterogeneity shifts the premelting onset toward the bulk melting point.
Conventional synthesis produces equiatomic nanoparticles with moderate natural surface segregation.
Elemental segregation creates locally weakened binding environments.
Locally weakened binding environments lower the energy barrier for surface melting.
Annealing produces a more uniform surface-energy landscape.
A more uniform surface-energy landscape raises the temperature required to initiate premelting.
Annealed nanoparticles will exhibit a statistically significant increase in premelting onset temperature relative to untreated nanoparticles.
Untreated nanoparticles premelt at lower temperatures because of natural surface segregation.
The proposed relationship applies to equiatomic high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles containing at least five principal elements and measuring 5–50 nm under inert atmosphere.
Nanoparticle shape, internal defects, and thermal history may also affect melting behavior.
